editorialSummary.text: Enduring diner dishing up breakfast & lunch classics in an old-fashioned atmosphere.

text.text:
Walking into Tom’s Restaurant feels like stepping into a place that never really changed, and that is kind of the charm. The booths are simple, the menu is straightforward, and everything moves at a calm diner pace. I ordered blueberry pancakes first and they came out fluffy and soft with a light sweetness that did not feel heavy.

The western omelet was next and it had that home cooked style with peppers, ham, and onions all folded together in a way that felt familiar. The French toast had a nice crisp edge but stayed soft inside, and it soaked up syrup without turning soggy too quickly. Coffee kept getting refilled without needing to ask which added to the comfort of the place.

It felt like the kind of spot you don’t overthink, you just settle in and eat slowly.

text.text:
The American Club started out as a dormitory for immigrant workers and now operates as one of the most well-regarded resorts in the Midwest, which is a pretty remarkable transformation when you think about it. Walking into the Tudor-style brick building, you get this immediate sense of old-world hospitality, the kind that feels deliberate rather than performative. We arrived as snow was falling lightly outside, and it set a tone for the whole stay that felt cozy and a little storybook.
Check-in was smooth, and we ended up getting a small upgrade to a nicer room without asking, which set a good tone right away. The rooms themselves were elegant without feeling stiff, comfortable beds, a quiet that made it easy to settle in after a day outside. We spent a good chunk of time at the Kohler Waters Spa, which is genuinely one of the best parts of staying here, the treatments were relaxing and the staff clearly know what they're doing. Dinner one evening leaned into a brunch-style spread with several dishes, and the food across the board was consistently well prepared, nothing flashy but executed with care. Our friends spent an afternoon at the Swing Suite trying out the golf simulator setup, which sounded like a fun way to spend time without needing actual golf weather.
Checkout was just as smooth as check-in, the valet team handled everything without us having to think twice about it, which is the kind of small detail that makes the whole stay feel effortless from start to finish.

I’ve been coming to Tom’s Diner for decades, but lately it’s lost some of its old-school charm. The atmosphere isn’t what it used to be, much louder now,  new residents pack the place with strollers, screaming babies and constant chatter making it feel more like a daycare than the classic Brooklyn diner I remember.

To be fair, the staff is still friendly and hospitable  and the last few times I went management even comped parts of my meals because of my dissatisfaction, which I appreciated.

That said, the food quality just hasn’t been the same. The final kicker for me was being served eggs with a perfectly recognizable, unmelted square of cheese just sitting on top. Also not the cheapest spot on the block anymore. Sad to say, it’s no longer my neighborhood go-to.

Nuaa Table was such a good last-minute Saturday night find for the four of us. The place has that cozy, welcoming vibe that makes you want to stay a little longer, but the service was still impressively fast, which honestly feels like a small miracle on a weekend.

The food felt special and a little different from the usual Thai menu. My 7-year-old decided to be unexpectedly adventurous, ordered the mee krob and the duck skewers, and ate all of it — including the spicy parts, which says a lot. The colossal crab curry noodle soup was a very generous portion and deeply satisfying, and the braised lamb special really stood out too.

Overall, this is the kind of place that feels both comforting and memorable — not just good dinner, but dinner you actually talk about after.

editorialSummary.text: Trendy, stylish spot serving Texas-style BBQ by the pound, plus sandwiches & Southern sides.

text.text:
This BBQ spot definitely had its highs and a few misses, but overall it’s a place worth checking out.

Starting with the sides, the cornbread was solid and a great way to kick things off. The greens were also well done, but the coleslaw didn’t quite hit the mark for me—it could’ve used a bit more oil and flavor. The beans were just okay, nothing too memorable.

For the meats, the chicken was decent but leaned a little too heavy on that smoky BBQ flavor for my taste. The pulled pork and brisket were both okay—the brisket had a nice texture but was lacking that deep flavor you hope for. I have a feeling these might shine more earlier in the day when everything is fresher.

Now, the standout: the ribs. Easily the best thing on the table—tender, flavorful, and exactly what you want from a good BBQ joint.

And don’t skip dessert—the seasonal apple pie was absolutely amazing and a perfect way to end the meal.

On top of that, the service really stood out. The servers were fantastic—friendly, attentive, and made the whole experience more enjoyable.

Overall, I’d definitely come back, but next time I’ll aim to get there earlier to catch everything at its best.

text.text:
Brighton Beach

There’s something special about bringing your child to a place that carries history on every plate.

Today I took my son to a traditional Eastern European café on Brighton Beach — a true corner of the former Soviet Union right here in Brooklyn. Walking under the elevated train tracks, hearing Russian spoken on every corner, seeing Cyrillic signs in the windows — it feels like stepping into another world.

And the food? Pure nostalgia.

We ordered classic dishes prepared the old way — the way they’ve been made for generations. Golden blintzes with sweet jam and sour cream, soft and perfectly pan-seared. A hearty omelet loaded with sausage, tomatoes, and mushrooms — simple, filling, honest food. Fresh bread in a basket, hot tea served in a traditional glass with a metal podstakannik holder — a detail that instantly brings back memories of train rides across Eastern Europe.

Nothing here is trendy. Nothing is over-styled.

It’s authentic.
It’s generous.
It’s rooted in tradition.

What makes Brighton Beach special is its multicultural blend — Russian, Ukrainian, Georgian, Uzbek, Jewish, Armenian influences — all living side by side, expressed through food that carries stories of migration, resilience, and identity.

Introducing my son to these flavors wasn’t just about breakfast.
It was about heritage.
It was about showing him where part of our culture comes from.
It was about keeping traditions alive.

The café may not be Michelin-starred.
But it serves something just as powerful — memory, warmth, and authenticity.

Brighton Beach never disappoints.

I work in fine dining and regularly visit a wide range of restaurants, but this was one of the worst dining experiences I’ve had. At over $300 per person plus tip, it was absolutely not worth the price. Very disappointing.

《Service & Experience Issues》

The lighting was flickering throughout the meal, making it difficult to relax.

Someone from the upstairs apartment repeatedly banged on the ceiling during service due to noise complaints. Police even showed up near the end of dinner.

There was no indication on Resy or the restaurant’s website of how long the tasting menu would take. I expected around 90 minutes, but the meal lasted over 3 hours, with about 20 minutes between courses.

The music was poorly curated—ranging from what sounded like Disney tracks to random 90s songs—with no cohesion, creating an uncomfortable atmosphere. Additionally, the volume was too loud, making it difficult to hear the server’s explanations of each dish. A quieter, more ambient style of music would be more appropriate.

There was no drink menu. Instead, a female server verbally listed all beverage options. As a guest, having a written menu would have been far more practical and transparent, especially to avoid repeatedly asking for prices.

The utensil holder appeared to be made from scented wood or incense-like material, and the smell transferred onto the forks and knives, affecting the taste and aroma of the food. When I brought this up, the server reacted defensively and unprofessionally.

After returning from the restroom, my napkin had not been refolded, which is a basic expectation in fine dining.

When I suggested that the restaurant should indicate the expected duration of the course on Resy or their website, the server responded dismissively, saying they’ve operated this way for 10 years and implying I shouldn’t question it.
